source_text:
The appearance of high entropy alloys breaks the traditional design concept of alloys based on mixing enthalpy and opens up a broad space for composition design for the research and development of new materials. The comprehensive effect of the mixing of various main elements endows the high entropy alloy with high entropy effect in thermodynamics, lattice distortion effect in structure, hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, and “cocktail” effect in performance. The principle of multi-principal element design based on these four effects results in the high entropy alloy showing many unique properties beyond the traditional alloy. These characteristics cover excellent corrosion resistance, wear resistance, excellent fatigue strength, and yield strength under various temperature conditions, high hardness, excellent microstructure stability and thermal stability, and excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance. In view of their outstanding mechanical and functional characteristics, high entropy alloys show broad application prospects in many fields, such as marine engineering, the automotive industry, energy development, the chemical industry, and biomedicine.

FeNiCrCo-X high entropy alloys have become a research hotspot for the relevant scholars in recent years because of their unique physical properties such as high temperature stability, high hardness, and high strength. Among them, FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy has excellent wear resistance, which is regarded as an ideal high-temperature wear-resistant material, attracting a large number of scholars to study such alloys. At present, it has been proven that this alloy can be achieved and is suitable for use as a thin film application. Due to the expensive preparation of this high entropy alloy material, it is more reasonable to add it as a coating material to traditional metal surfaces in future practical applications. A new Al0.75CrFeNi eutectic high entropy alloy was prepared composed of a disordered body centered cubic phase and an ordered body centered cubic (BCC) phase, showing excellent mechanical properties and high yield strength. Mohsen et al.  systematically studied the wear resistance of the AlxCo1.5CrFeNil.5Tiy system and found that the wear resistance of Col.5CrFeNil.5Ti and A10.2Co1.5CrFeNil.5Ti alloys was at least twice that of conventional wear-resistant steel. Braic et al.  used (TiZrNbHfTa)N high entropy alloy as a protective coating in the biomedical field to improve the indicators of titanium alloy implants; they pointed out that the hardness of the alloy increased to 30 GPa, and the surface wear rate was lower than 0.2 × 10−6 mm3 N−1 m−1. Li et al.  found that FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating on the surface of a Cu matrix can effectively improve the wear resistance of the material by the molecular dynamics method. They reached the conclusion that an increase of the friction velocity results in the reduction of the tangential force affected by material thermal softening and the increase of the normal force affected by material strain rate hardening, and therefore leads to the reduction of the friction coefficient. Yang et al.  found that the hardness and Young’s modulus of AlCoCrFe high entropy alloy coatings are about 10 times that of the substrate metal Al. In the interface area between the high entropy alloy coating and the Al substrate, due to the laser heating during the manufacturing process of the high entropy alloy coating, a part of the substrate melts and reacts with other elements in the coating forming several BCC structures which can effectively protect the matrix material from wear.. Doan et al., using AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy as a coating material adhered to the surface of a Ni substrate, found that Ni based alloys are protected by high entropy alloy coatings with less wear. With the increase of friction depth, the resistance of tool movement is greater, and the friction coefficient increases. Instead, due to the effects of thermal softening and strain rate hardening, the friction coefficient decreases with the increase of friction speed. Bui et al.  investigated the effects of composition, grain size, and cutting depth on the deformation behavior and damage of NiCoCrFe high entropy alloys. It was found that the dislocations increased with the increase of Co content, the Ni25Co25Cr25Fe25 high entropy alloy had the highest number of worn atoms, while the Ni25Co25Cr30Fe20 high entropy alloy had the lowest number of worn atoms.

It can be concluded that researchers have mainly focused on studying the room temperature friction performance of high entropy alloy materials and have not studied the overall wear resistance at different temperatures. However, at present, researchers are mainly focusing on the study of the properties of the materials themselves and are not studying their overall wear resistance as coating materials. Also, it is difficult to observe the microscopic deformation mechanism during the experimental process, and effective conclusions cannot be drawn on the impact mechanism of wear resistance at different temperatures.

queries.broad: For high-entropy-alloy coatings used in wear-resistant applications, what single intervention could improve wear resistance across operating temperatures? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise identical unmodified coating, the temperature and sliding conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.
queries.problem_constrained: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, whose overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior across different temperatures remain unclear, what single intervention could improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions, defines the operating limits of the prediction, cites supporting evidence from the introduction, and proposes a falsification experiment capable of resolving microscopic deformation during wear.
queries.expert_context: FeNiCrCoCu is considered a promising high-temperature wear-resistant alloy, is suitable for thin-film use, and is more practical as a coating than as a bulk material because of preparation cost. Prior work reported improved wear resistance for FeNiCrCoCu coatings on Cu matrices and linked friction-velocity effects to thermal softening and strain-rate hardening. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, titanium-alloy, or other substrates also reported improved hardness or reduced wear, while composition, grain size, cutting depth, friction speed, and friction depth were found to affect deformation or friction. Nevertheless, most studies addressed room-temperature behavior, often emphasized the alloys themselves rather than their overall performance as coatings, and could not directly resolve microscopic deformation at different temperatures. Subject to retaining the coating format and practical rationale, what single intervention could improve the overall wear resistance of a FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix across different temperatures? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the causal microscopic mechanism, the predicted change relative to an unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating under matched tests, the temperatures and sliding conditions delimiting validity, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and an experiment whose measurements and rejection criterion could falsify both the predicted wear improvement and the proposed mechanism.

queries.expert_context: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.
